title: Impact of elemental segregation on active and transpassive corrosion phenomenology of additively manufactured 316L - npj Materials Degradation
byline: Montoya; Timothy; Macatangay; Duane; Kelly; Robert G
html:
Abstract

The active and transpassive dissolution behaviors of additively manufactured (AM) laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and direct energy deposition (DED) 316L stainless steels were evaluated using ASTM standard methods as well as electrochemical and microscopy characterization techniques. Conventional wrought 316L and 317L was used as baselines for chemical, microstructure, and electrochemical behavior. It was discovered that both LPBF and DED induce non-equilibrium solidification conditions that lead to elemental segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mo. The segregation occurs at cellular dendritic walls in LPBF and within the ferrite phase in DED, whereas wrought materials exhibit a homogeneous microstructure and elemental distribution. Under active dissolution in the presence of acidic (H2SO4) and depassivating species (KSCN), cellular dendritic interiors and melt pool boundaries undergo selective attack in LPBF while austenite dissolves faster than ferrite in DED. Conversely, when transpassive dissolution occurs, cellular dendritic walls are attacked in LPBF, and ferrite is attacked in DED. When LPBF processing parameters are optimized for density, the corrosion rate (ASTM A262 Practice B) was the lowest in comparison to wrought 316L and 317L. Samples with the highest corrosion rate correlated to the presence of lack-of-fusion porosity (1.8% porosity) or a large grain structure (DED).
